Intro to Machine Learning; Linear Regression Models

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold

Music Challenge

Which popular songs from the past will be recognized by future generations, and which will fade into obscurity? The website The Pudding conducts the Music Challenge where they ask thousands of people whether they recognize hit songs from the past. We’ll look at some of the data related to the article “Defining the 90s Music Canon”.

The data set at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/song-decay-clean/refs/heads/master/src/assets/data/lollipop_chart_data_july_13.csv contains 344 songs released in the 1990s. For each song, the proportion of survey respondents who recognized the song is recorded, for both Millennial respondents and Gen Z respondents. Our goal will be to use linear regression to predict the Gen Z recognition.

We will try several different linear regression models. Save each of your models with a different name because you will compare them at the end.

  1. Read in the data and describe the Gen Z recognition variable.
music = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/song-decay-clean/refs/heads/master/src/assets/data/lollipop_chart_data_july_13.csv")

  1. Use scikit-learn to fit a linear regression model for predicting Gen Z recognition from Millennial recognition.
X_music = music[["mean_millennial_recognition"]]
y_music = music["mean_gen_z_recognition"]

linear_model = LinearRegression()
linear_model.fit(X_music, y_music)

print("slope:", linear_model.coef_[0])
print("intercept:", linear_model.intercept_)
print("R-squared:", linear_model.score(X_music, y_music))

x_grid = np.linspace(X_music.min().iloc[0], X_music.max().iloc[0], 200).reshape(-1, 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.scatter(X_music, y_music, alpha=0.7)
plt.plot(x_grid, linear_model.predict(x_grid), color="crimson", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Millennial recognition")
plt.ylabel("Gen Z recognition")
plt.title("Gen Z recognition predicted by Millennial recognition")
plt.show()

The straight line misses the shape of the data. The points curve upward: Gen Z recognition stays low until Millennial recognition is fairly high, then rises steeply. So the line overpredicts in the middle and underpredicts the best-known songs. Its intercept is negative, and it predicts a negative recognition, which is impossible, for the 11 songs with Millennial recognition below about 0.07.

  1. Explain why you might want to consider taking a log of Gen Z recognition. Then use scikit-learn to fit a linear regression model for predicting log of Gen Z recognition from Millennial recognition.
# Gen Z recognition is a proportion between 0 and 1 and is right-skewed.
# Taking a log can make the relationship less curved and reduce the influence of very large values.
log_model = LinearRegression()
log_model.fit(X_music, np.log(y_music))

print("slope:", log_model.coef_[0])
print("intercept:", log_model.intercept_)
print("R-squared for log(Gen Z recognition):", log_model.score(X_music, np.log(y_music)))
slope: 2.7991680362225217
intercept: -2.9082912239452847
R-squared for log(Gen Z recognition): 0.8230294902084205

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.scatter(X_music, y_music, alpha=0.7)
plt.plot(x_grid, np.exp(log_model.predict(x_grid)), color="darkorange", linewidth=2)
plt.xlabel("Millennial recognition")
plt.ylabel("Gen Z recognition")
plt.title("Log model, transformed back to Gen Z recognition")
plt.show()

  1. Choose one of your favorite songs that is in the data set. Use each model to predict the Gen Z recognition for the song. Which model gives the best prediction?
favorite = music[music["artist_song"].str.contains("No Scrubs", case=False, na=False)].copy()

favorite_x = favorite[["mean_millennial_recognition"]]

favorite_x_square = pd.DataFrame({
    "millennial_recognition": favorite_x["mean_millennial_recognition"],
    "millennial_recognition_squared": favorite_x["mean_millennial_recognition"] ** 2,
})

favorite_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "actual Gen Z recognition": favorite["mean_gen_z_recognition"].values,
    "linear prediction": linear_model.predict(favorite_x),
    "log-model prediction": np.exp(log_model.predict(favorite_x)),
    "quadratic prediction": square_model.predict(favorite_x_square),
}, index=favorite["artist_song"])

for model in ["linear prediction", "log-model prediction", "quadratic prediction"]:
    favorite_results[f"{model} error"] = (
        favorite_results[model] - favorite_results["actual Gen Z recognition"]
    ).abs()

My song is “No Scrubs” by TLC. The log model gave the best prediction because it predicted a Gen Z recognition of 0.6646, which was only 0.0025 away from the actual value. The quadratic model was also close, but the linear model had the largest error and underpredicted this popular song.

nirvana_x = pd.DataFrame({"mean_millennial_recognition": [0.7]})
nirvana_x_square = pd.DataFrame({

    "millennial_recognition_squared": [0.7 ** 2],
})

nirvana_predictions = pd.Series({

Name: predicted Gen Z recognition, dtype: float64

For “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” the linear model predicts 0.447, the log model predicts 0.387, and the quadratic model predicts 0.418. Since the song is not in the data, there is no actual Gen Z recognition value, so I cannot know for sure which model is best. I would choose the log model because similar songs with Millennial recognition close to 0.7 had an average Gen Z recognition of about 0.388, which is almost exactly the log model’s prediction.

Categorical Predictors (FEV data)

Do non-smokers have better lungs than smokers? One measure of lung function is forced expiratory volume (FEV), the amount of air (in liters) an individual can exhale in the first second of forceful breath. Larger values of FEV are indicative of better functioning lungs. In a study, FEV was measured for a group of 654 subjects, along with whether or not they smoked and other variables.

1. First fit a regression model with a single predictor: Smoking status. Since this variable is categorical you need to “dummify” it before fitting the model.

smoke_dummy = pd.get_dummies(df_fev["Smoking status"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)
smoke_model = LinearRegression()
smoke_model.fit(smoke_dummy, df_fev["FEV"])

print("dummy-variable column:", smoke_dummy.columns.tolist())
print("coefficient:", smoke_model.coef_[0])
print("intercept:", smoke_model.intercept_)
dummy-variable column: ['smoker']

2. What are the predictions from this model? How could we have known that those would be the predictions?

group_means = df_fev.groupby("Smoking status")["FEV"].mean()
predictions_by_group = pd.DataFrame({
    "Smoking status": ["non-smoker", "smoker"],
    "predicted FEV": smoke_model.predict(pd.DataFrame({"smoker": [0, 1]})),
})

display(group_means)
display(predictions_by_group)

Name: FEV, dtype: float64
Smoking status predicted FEV
0 non-smoker 2.566143

The model predicts 2.57 L for every non-smoker and 3.27 L for every smoker. These are just the average FEV values for each group. Since smoking status is the only predictor, the model gives one average prediction for non-smokers and one for smokers.

3. Look at the results for the previous parts. What do you notice? Is this what you expected? Remember: larger FEV means better lungs - who tends to have larger FEV, smokers or non-smokers?

Smokers have a higher average FEV than non-smokers: 3.28 L compared with 2.57 L. This was not what I expected because smoking is harmful to the lungs. Smoking status alone does not explain why this happened, so other factors, like age, may be affecting the results.

4. Suggest some explanations for why smokers tend to have higher FEV than non-smokers?

The smokers are probably older and taller than the non-smokers, which means they naturally have larger lungs and higher FEV. Smoking is likely not improving their lungs the simple model is missing important factors like age and body size. There are also fewer smokers in the data, and they may have only been smoking for a short time.

7. Fit a linear regression model with predictors smoking status, Age, and their interaction.

df_fev["Age (years)"] = df_fev["Age (months)"] / 12

X_int = pd.get_dummies(
    df_fev[["Smoking status"]],
    drop_first=True,
    dtype=int
)

X_int["Age (years)"] = df_fev["Age (years)"]
X_int["smoker_x_age"] = (
    X_int["Smoking status_smoker"] * X_int["Age (years)"]
)

y_fev = df_fev["FEV"]

interaction_model = LinearRegression()
interaction_model.fit(X_int, y_fev)

coefs = pd.Series(interaction_model.coef_, index=X_int.columns)

print(coefs)
print("Intercept:", round(interaction_model.intercept_, 4))
print("R-squared:", round(interaction_model.score(X_int, y_fev), 4))

print(
    "\nNon-smoker line: FEV =",
    round(interaction_model.intercept_, 3),
    "+",
    round(coefs["Age (years)"], 3),
    "× age"
)

print(
    "Smoker line: FEV =",
    round(interaction_model.intercept_ + coefs["Smoking status_smoker"], 3),
    "+",
    round(coefs["Age (years)"] + coefs["smoker_x_age"], 3),
    "× age"
)

9. Compare the models. Which do you think is “best”? Why? How could you investigate?

The smoking-only model is the worst because it ignores age, which is an important reason why FEV changes. I think the interaction model is the best because it has the highest (R^2) and the lowest cross-validation error, but its improvement over the smoking + age model is small. I could investigate more by testing the models on a held-out set or repeating cross-validation to see if the interaction model consistently performs better.
